cases.final_diagnosis: CNC-02 has a developing mechanical problem, most likely spindle-bearing wear/deterioration (or related imbalance/looseness), causing vibration to repeatedly exceed the 4.50 mm/s alarm setpoint while the machine runs. The vibration spiked to 4.58 mm/s at tick 914 and again 4.51 mm/s at tick 919 (E4), and remained elevated through tick 930 with repeated crossings above 4.50 (ticks 922, 926, 928 in E9). Load (E5) and temperature (E6) stayed stable, ruling out an operating-change or thermal cause, and CNC-02 is confirmed running with job 12 (E11). Other machines show normal vibration (E10, E12), so this is localized to CNC-02, not a line-wide issue.

Jobs 11, 13, and 15 (all in batch 2) failed inspection, while jobs 12 and 14 in the same batch passed, and all ten batch-1 jobs passed. The failures alternate within batch 2 (fail-pass-fail-pass-fail), which argues against a uniform cause: a defective station such as CNC-06 would affect every job passing through it (jobs 12 and 14 also went through CNC-06 and passed), a uniform batch/material issue would not spare jobs 12 and 14, and a uniform speed/setting error would likewise not alternate job to job. No alarms or per-station timing anomaly have yet been isolated. Current evidence best fits inspection randomness / coincidental multiple causes (H4), but confidence is low because I have not compared the passing batch-2 jobs' per-station timings or checked for alarms/maintenance events. None of the hypotheses approaches the 0.90 confidence needed to approve an intervention, and no available action (bearing replacement, speed reset, servo drive, hydraulics repair) would address randomness.

Three of four batch-1 jobs failed inspection after CNC-05 (the last station before inspection); only job 3 passed. CNC-05 following_error during each job's time at CNC-05 shows the passing job (job 3) had the lowest error (mean 2.572, max 3.586) while the three failing jobs ran with higher error (job 1: mean 3.252/max 5.046; job 2: mean 3.686/max 5.516; job 4: mean 2.909/max 4.15). This is consistent with H1 (a CNC-05 axis/servo fault producing out-of-tolerance parts) but is not conclusive — job 4's error is only moderately elevated, so a material-variation cause (H2) remains possible. No recent intervention or maintenance explains the shift (H4 contradicted by E4/E9), and a batch-wide cause is contradicted by job 3 passing (H3 contradicted by E7). Confidence is too low to intervene (needs ≥0.90).

CNC-01 had a brief, self-resolving vibration spike: vibration exceeded the 4.50 mm/s alarm setpoint for exactly four ticks (521-524, peaking at 7.37 mm/s) and then returned to the ~2.0-2.5 mm/s baseline by tick 525, remaining normal through tick 540. There was no correlated change in load (~66-69%), temperature (~120-126°F), or following error (~3-4 µm during the spike versus ~4-6 µm baseline), neighboring CNC-02 was unaffected, and the maintenance history shows no pending bearing, spindle, or sensor issues. This is consistent with a transient, non-recurring event rather than a developing mechanical fault, so no factory change is required.

CNC-03 experienced a transient vibration burst during ticks 71-78 (peaking at 5.21 mm/s, above the 4.50 mm/s alarm threshold) that has fully resolved. Vibration returned to normal by tick 79 (0.37 mm/s) and remained normal through tick 90 (all readings at or below ~0.36 mm/s). During the burst there was no load change (E4 load near 0%), no temperature spike (E8), no other alarms, stops, or job movements (E6), and CNC-03 is now idle (E10). This is a non-recurring transient disturbance, not a persistent mechanical fault such as bearing deterioration or imbalance. The exact trigger (spindle spin-down/up or external bump) is not recorded in the available data, but it does not affect the diagnosis because the condition has cleared and is not recurring.
